claim: The type VI secretion system (T6SS) is used by bacteria to deliver toxic effectors directly into target cells.
source: The type VI secretion system (T6SS) is used by bacteria to deliver toxic effectors directly into target cells.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about T6SS function.

claim: Most T6SSs mediate antibacterial activities.
source: Most T6SSs mediate antibacterial activities, whereas the potential anti-eukaryotic role of T6SS remains understudied.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: The potential anti-eukaryotic role of T6SS remains understudied.
source: Most T6SSs mediate antibacterial activities, whereas the potential anti-eukaryotic role of T6SS remains understudied.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of research in the field.

claim: A Vibrio T6SS delivers two novel effectors into mammalian host immune cells.
source: Here, we found a Vibrio T6SS that delivers two novel effectors into mammalian host immune cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: T6SS effectors induce pyroptotic cell death in a phagocytosis-dependent manner.
source: We showed that these effectors induce a pyroptotic cell death in a phagocytosis-dependent manner
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing cell death requires phagocytosis.

claim: The NLRP3 inflammasome is the underlying mechanism leading to T6SS-induced pyroptosis.
source: we identified the NLRP3 inflammasome as being the underlying mechanism leading to the T6SS-induced pyroptosis.
evidence: This is supported by genetic experiments using Nlrp3-/- mice.

claim: A compensatory T6SS-induced pathway is activated upon inhibition of the canonical pyroptosis pathway.
source: Moreover, we identified a compensatory T6SS-induced pathway that is activated upon inhibition of the canonical pyroptosis pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with Gsdmd-/- BMDMs showing alternative cell death mechanisms.

claim: This T6SS and its anti-eukaryotic effectors may have spread via horizontal gene transfer into emerging pathogens in the marine environment.
source: Genetic analyses revealed possible horizontal spread of this T6SS and its anti-eukaryotic effectors into emerging pathogens in the marine environment.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis showing similar T6SS clusters in other bacteria near DNA mobility elements.

claim: Innate immune responses combat infections but may also drive pathological inflammation.
source: Innate immune responses combat infections but may also drive pathological inflammation.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the dual role of innate immunity.

claim: Pattern-recognition receptors (PRRs) are expressed by cells at the defensive front line against infections including macrophages, dendritic cells, and neutrophils.
source: The innate immune system engages an array of pattern-recognition receptors (PRR) that are expressed by cells found at the defensive front line against infections including macrophages, dendritic cells, neutrophils, and others.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about innate immune cell types.

claim: PRRs can detect pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs).
source: PRRs can detect a variety of microbial determinants termed pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about PRR function.

claim: Damaged host cells can trigger PRRs by releasing danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs).
source: Moreover, damaged host cells can also trigger PRRs by releasing danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) (Wallach et al., 2014; Wen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Some PRRs of the innate immune system are assembled into a high-molecular weight complex called 'the inflammasome' after sensing DAMPs or PAMPs.
source: Some PRRs of the innate immune system are assembled into a high-molecular weight complex called 'the inflammasome' after sensing DAMPs or PAMPs.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about inflammasome assembly.

claim: Inflammasome complexes can kill an infected cell through pyroptosis.
source: Inflammasome complexes are considered central components of innate immunity because of their ability to kill an infected cell (a cell death process that is termed pyroptosis), or by their activation and the subsequent secretion of mature proinflammatory cytokines interleukin 1β (IL-1β) and IL-18 (Lamkanfi and Dixit, 2014; Schroder and Tschopp, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inflammasome activation leads to secretion of mature proinflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18.
source: Inflammasome complexes are considered central components of innate immunity because of their ability to kill an infected cell (a cell death process that is termed pyroptosis), or by their activation and the subsequent secretion of mature proinflammatory cytokines interleukin 1β (IL-1β) and IL-18 (Lamkanfi and Dixit, 2014; Schroder and Tschopp, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inflammasomes can be divided into canonical and non-canonical pathways.
source: Inflammasomes can be divided into: (1) a canonical pathway in which Caspase-1 is cleaved into a catalytically active enzyme, and (2) non-canonical pathways in which Caspase-11 is activated (Lamkanfi and Dixit, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The canonical inflammasome pathway involves Caspase-1 cleavage into a catalytically active enzyme.
source: Inflammasomes can be divided into: (1) a canonical pathway in which Caspase-1 is cleaved into a catalytically active enzyme, and (2) non-canonical pathways in which Caspase-11 is activated (Lamkanfi and Dixit, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Non-canonical inflammasome pathways involve Caspase-11 activation.
source: Inflammasomes can be divided into: (1) a canonical pathway in which Caspase-1 is cleaved into a catalytically active enzyme, and (2) non-canonical pathways in which Caspase-11 is activated (Lamkanfi and Dixit, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The canonical inflammasome comprises NLR family members including NLRP1, NLRP3, NLRC4, or AIM2.
source: The canonical inflammasome comprises one of the nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain (NOD), leucine-rich repeat (LRR)-containing protein (NLR) family members, including NLRP1, NLRP3, NLRC4, or the DNA sensor absent in melanoma 2 (AIM2), all of which contain either a pyrin domain (PYD) or a caspase recruitment domain (CARD) (Schroder and Tschopp, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: NLR family members contain either a pyrin domain (PYD) or a caspase recruitment domain (CARD).
source: The canonical inflammasome comprises one of the nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain (NOD), leucine-rich repeat (LRR)-containing protein (NLR) family members, including NLRP1, NLRP3, NLRC4, or the DNA sensor absent in melanoma 2 (AIM2), all of which contain either a pyrin domain (PYD) or a caspase recruitment domain (CARD) (Schroder and Tschopp, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: NLR domains interact with ASC, leading to its polymerization into ASC specks.
source: These domains interact with apoptosis-associated speck-like protein (ASC), leading to its polymerization into large helical filaments known as ASC specks by facilitating self-interactions of the PYD of ASC (Franklin et al., 2014; Proell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The CARD domain of ASC specks recruits Caspase-1 via CARD-CARD interaction.
source: The CARD domain of the ASC specks recruits Caspase-1 via a CARD-CARD interaction, leading to Caspase-1 clustering that permits autocleavage and formation of the active Caspase-1 p10/p20 tetramer (Lamkanfi and Dixit, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Caspase-1 clustering permits autocleavage and formation of the active Caspase-1 p10/p20 tetramer.
source: The CARD domain of the ASC specks recruits Caspase-1 via a CARD-CARD interaction, leading to Caspase-1 clustering that permits autocleavage and formation of the active Caspase-1 p10/p20 tetramer (Lamkanfi and Dixit, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Activated Caspase-1 processes pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their mature forms.
source: Activated Caspase-1 processes pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their mature forms.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Caspase-1 function.

claim: Activated Caspase-1 cleaves gasdermin D (GSDMD) into C-terminal and N-terminal fragments.
source: Simultaneously, activated Caspase-1 cleaves gasdermin D (GSDMD) into a C-terminal fragment (GSDMD-CT) and N-terminal fragment (GSDMD-NT) (Liu et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GSDMD-NT oligomerizes in membranes to form pores which promote IL-1β release and pyroptotic cell death.
source: GSDMD-NT oligomerizes in membranes to form pores which promote IL-1β release and pyroptotic cell death (Lieberman et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: T6SS is a widespread macromolecular protein secretion apparatus that translocates proteins into neighboring cells in a contact-dependent manner.
source: The type VI secretion system (T6SS) is a widespread macromolecular protein secretion apparatus that translocates proteins into neighboring cells in a contact-dependent manner (Bingle et al., 2008; Boyer et al., 2009; Mougous et al., 2006; Pukatzki et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Most T6SS-secreted proteins are toxic effectors capable of manipulating target cells.
source: Most of the T6SS-secreted proteins are toxic effectors capable of manipulating target cells.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about T6SS effectors.

claim: Many T6SS effectors are antibacterial toxins.
source: Although many T6SS effectors are antibacterial toxins, some T6SSs deliver effectors with anti-eukaryotic activities into host cells, thus promoting virulence or defense against predation (Monjarás Feria and Valvano, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Some T6SSs deliver effectors with anti-eukaryotic activities into host cells, promoting virulence or defense against predation.
source: Although many T6SS effectors are antibacterial toxins, some T6SSs deliver effectors with anti-eukaryotic activities into host cells, thus promoting virulence or defense against predation (Monjarás Feria and Valvano, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The anti-eukaryotic potential of T6SSs remains understudied and possibly underappreciated.
source: Nevertheless, the anti-eukaryotic potential of T6SSs remains understudied and possibly underappreciated (Dar et al., 2018; Hachani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: T6SS is common in vibrios.
source: T6SS is common in vibrios (Dar et al., 2018), a genus of Gram-negative marine bacteria that includes many established and emerging human pathogens (e.g. Vibrio cholerae, Vibrio parahaemolyticus, and Vibrio vulnificus), which are a leading cause of gastroenteritis and wound infections (Baker-Austin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Vibrios include many established and emerging human pathogens such as V. cholerae, V. parahaemolyticus, and V. vulnificus.
source: T6SS is common in vibrios (Dar et al., 2018), a genus of Gram-negative marine bacteria that includes many established and emerging human pathogens (e.g. Vibrio cholerae, Vibrio parahaemolyticus, and Vibrio vulnificus), which are a leading cause of gastroenteritis and wound infections (Baker-Austin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Vibrios are a leading cause of gastroenteritis and wound infections.
source: T6SS is common in vibrios (Dar et al., 2018), a genus of Gram-negative marine bacteria that includes many established and emerging human pathogens (e.g. Vibrio cholerae, Vibrio parahaemolyticus, and Vibrio vulnificus), which are a leading cause of gastroenteritis and wound infections (Baker-Austin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Vibrios preferentially grow in warm (>15°C) marine environments.
source: Vibrios preferentially grow in warm (>15°C) marine environments; remarkably, the rise in sea surface temperatures correlates with the spread of vibrios and with Vibrio-associated human illness (Le Roux et al., 2015; Vezzulli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The rise in sea surface temperatures correlates with the spread of vibrios and with Vibrio-associated human illness.
source: Vibrios preferentially grow in warm (>15°C) marine environments; remarkably, the rise in sea surface temperatures correlates with the spread of vibrios and with Vibrio-associated human illness (Le Roux et al., 2015; Vezzulli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: V. proteolyticus is a Gram-negative marine bacterium originally isolated from the intestine of the wood borer Limnoria tripunctata.
source: Vibrio proteolyticus (V. proteolyticus) is a Gram-negative marine bacterium that was originally isolated from the intestine of the wood borer Limnoria tripunctata (Merkel et al., 1964)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: V. proteolyticus was isolated from diseased corals.
source: it was also isolated from diseased corals (Cervino et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: V. proteolyticus causes mortality in fish.
source: and was shown to cause mortality in fish (Bowden et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: V. proteolyticus causes mortality in the crustacean model organism Artemia.
source: and in the crustacean model organism, Artemia (Verschuere et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: V. proteolyticus does not possess a type III secretion system (T3SS).
source: V. proteolyticus does not possess a type III secretion system (T3SS) that can mediate delivery of effector proteins directly into host cells (Miller et al., 2019; Ray et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: V. proteolyticus encodes a secreted pore-forming hemolysin.
source: Nevertheless, it encodes a secreted pore-forming hemolysin (Cohen et al., 2020; Ray et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: V. proteolyticus encodes three different T6SSs (T6SS1-3).
source: and three different T6SSs (T6SS1-3) (Ray et al., 2016; Ray et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: T6SS1 mediates both antibacterial and anti-eukaryotic activities.
source: T6SS1 mediates both antibacterial and anti-eukaryotic activities, whereas T6SS3 does not play any role in bacterial competition and its hypothesized anti-eukaryotic potential remains to be investigated (Ray et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: T6SS3 does not play any role in bacterial competition.
source: T6SS1 mediates both antibacterial and anti-eukaryotic activities, whereas T6SS3 does not play any role in bacterial competition and its hypothesized anti-eukaryotic potential remains to be investigated (Ray et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: V. proteolyticus induces VPRH-independent cell death in primary macrophages but not in HeLa or RAW264.7 cell lines.
source: In a recent study in which we investigated the secreted V. proteolyticus cytotoxic hemolysin, VPRH, we observed the existence of another, VPRH-independent cell death that occurred only during infections of primary macrophages, but not in the cultured cell lines HeLa or RAW264.7 (Cohen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Deletion of hns1 resulted in elevated secretion of both VgrG1 and Hcp3 compared to the parental Δvprh strain.
source: We found that hns1 deletion resulted in elevated secretion of both VgrG1 and Hcp3, compared to their secretion from the parental Δvprh strain (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The secretion of VgrG1 and Hcp3 was T6SS1- and T6SS3-dependent, respectively.
source: Notably, the secretion of VgrG1 and Hcp3 was T6SS1- and T6SS3-dependent, respectively, as evident from their absence in the supernatant fractions of strains deleted for tssG1 (T6SS1-) and tssL3 (T6SS3-), which are core structural genes required for the activity of T6SS1 and T6SS3, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data showing absence of secretion in deletion mutants.

claim: hns1 deletion derepresses T6SS1 and T6SS3, leading to their constitutive activation and elevated secretion.
source: These results indicate that hns1 deletion derepresses T6SS1 and T6SS3, leading to their constitutive activation and thus elevated secretion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed elevated secretion data.

claim: Infection with the Δvprh strain resulted in negligible cell death 3 hr post infection.
source: Whereas, infection with the Δvprh strain resulted in negligible cell death 3 hr post infection, the Δvprh/Δhns1 mutant induced a rapid cell death in which ~80% of the cells in the culture were dead within this time frame (set as 100% Normalized Area Under the Curve [AUC]; Figure 1b and c).
evidence: This is supported by real-time microscopy data shown in Figure 1b and c.

claim: The Δvprh/Δhns1 mutant induced rapid cell death in which ~80% of cells were dead within 3 hours.
source: Whereas, infection with the Δvprh strain resulted in negligible cell death 3 hr post infection, the Δvprh/Δhns1 mutant induced a rapid cell death in which ~80% of the cells in the culture were dead within this time frame (set as 100% Normalized Area Under the Curve [AUC]; Figure 1b and c).
evidence: This is supported by real-time microscopy data shown in Figure 1b and c.

claim: The rapid cell death in the Δvprh/Δhns1 mutant was completely abrogated upon genetic inactivation of T6SS3.
source: Remarkably, the rapid cell death evident in the Δvprh/Δhns1 mutant was completely abrogated upon genetic inactivation of T6SS3 (Δvprh/Δhns1/T6SS3-), but not upon genetic inactivation of T6SS1 (Δvprh/Δhns1/T6SS1-) (Figure 1b and c).
evidence: This is supported by real-time microscopy data shown in Figure 1b and c.

claim: Genetic inactivation of T6SS1 did not abrogate the rapid cell death in the Δvprh/Δhns1 mutant.
source: Remarkably, the rapid cell death evident in the Δvprh/Δhns1 mutant was completely abrogated upon genetic inactivation of T6SS3 (Δvprh/Δhns1/T6SS3-), but not upon genetic inactivation of T6SS1 (Δvprh/Δhns1/T6SS1-) (Figure 1b and c).
evidence: This is supported by real-time microscopy data shown in Figure 1b and c.

claim: Genetic inactivation of T6SS1 or T6SS3 had no significant effect on bacterial growth in MLB or DMEM media.
source: Notably, genetic inactivation of T6SS1 or T6SS3 had no significant effect on growth during the relevant time frame compared to the parental Δvprh/Δhns1 strain in either marine lysogeny broth (MLB) or Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) media (Figure 1d)
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Genetic inactivation of T6SS1 or T6SS3 did not affect bacterial swimming motility.
source: nor did it affect bacterial swimming motility (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is supported by swimming motility data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: T6SS3, but not T6SS1, mediates VPRH-independent cell death in BMDMs.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that T6SS3, but not T6SS1, mediates a VPRH-independent cell death in BMDMs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic deletion experiments.

claim: Addition of MCC950 resulted in delayed and reduced cell death during infection with Δvprh/Δhns1 bacteria (~40% reduction).
source: Using real-time microscopy, we observed that addition of either inhibitors, MCC950 (blocks ASC oligomerization by inhibiting the canonical and non-canonical NLRP3 inflammasome Shao et al., 2015) or Vx765 (a potent and selective competitive inhibitor of Caspase-1 Church et al., 2008) resulted in delayed and reduced cell death during infection with Δvprh/Δhns1 bacteria (~40% reduction as measured by calculating the AUC), compared with a dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)-treated control (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: This is supported by real-time microscopy data shown in Figure 2a and b.

claim: Addition of Vx765 resulted in delayed and reduced cell death during infection with Δvprh/Δhns1 bacteria (~40% reduction).
source: Using real-time microscopy, we observed that addition of either inhibitors, MCC950 (blocks ASC oligomerization by inhibiting the canonical and non-canonical NLRP3 inflammasome Shao et al., 2015) or Vx765 (a potent and selective competitive inhibitor of Caspase-1 Church et al., 2008) resulted in delayed and reduced cell death during infection with Δvprh/Δhns1 bacteria (~40% reduction as measured by calculating the AUC), compared with a dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)-treated control (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: This is supported by real-time microscopy data shown in Figure 2a and b.

claim: Inactivation of T6SS3 abrogated the cell death phenotype.
source: As expected, inactivation of T6SS1 had no effect on Δvprh/Δhns1-induced cell death nor on the protective effect of the inhibitors, whereas inactivation of T6SS3 abrogated the cell death phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by real-time microscopy data.

claim: T6SS3 induces cell death in BMDMs via an inflammasome-dependent pyroptotic pathway.
source: These results support our hypothesis that T6SS3 induces cell death in BMDMs via an inflammasome-dependent pyroptotic pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the inhibitor experiments.

claim: IL-1β cleavage and secretion were dependent on the presence of a functional T6SS3 in Δvprh/Δhns1 strains.
source: As shown in Figure 2c–e, IL-1β cleavage and secretion were dependent on the presence of a functional T6SS3 in Δvprh/Δhns1 strains, and they were inhibited (Figure 2c) or undetected (Figure 2d and e) when inflammasome inhibitors were added.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA and immunoblot data shown in Figure 2c-e.

claim: IL-1β cleavage and secretion were inhibited or undetected when inflammasome inhibitors were added.
source: As shown in Figure 2c–e, IL-1β cleavage and secretion were dependent on the presence of a functional T6SS3 in Δvprh/Δhns1 strains, and they were inhibited (Figure 2c) or undetected (Figure 2d and e) when inflammasome inhibitors were added.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA and immunoblot data shown in Figure 2c-e.

claim: Secretion of TNFα was independent of T6SS3 activity and unaffected by addition of inflammasome inhibitors.
source: However, secretion of TNFα (an NF-κB-dependent, inflammasome-independent cytokine) was independent of T6SS3 activity and was unaffected by addition of inflammasome inhibitors (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Cleavage and release of Caspase-1 and GSDMD were apparent upon infection of BMDMs with the Δvprh/Δhns1 strain.
source: Additional hallmark pyroptotic processes, such as the cleavage and release of Caspase-1 and GSDMD, were apparent upon infection of BMDMs with the Δvprh/Δhns1 strain; however, they were undetected upon inactivation of T6SS3 or upon the addition of inflammasome inhibitors (Figure 2d and e).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2d and e.

claim: Cleavage and release of Caspase-1 and GSDMD were undetected upon inactivation of T6SS3 or upon addition of inflammasome inhibitors.
source: Additional hallmark pyroptotic processes, such as the cleavage and release of Caspase-1 and GSDMD, were apparent upon infection of BMDMs with the Δvprh/Δhns1 strain; however, they were undetected upon inactivation of T6SS3 or upon the addition of inflammasome inhibitors (Figure 2d and e).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2d and e.

claim: The death of BMDMs derived from Nlrp1-/- mice was comparable to that of BMDMs generated from WT mice.
source: Using real-time microscopy, we found that the death of BMDMs derived from Nlrp1-/- mice was comparable to that of BMDMs generated from WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by real-time microscopy data.

claim: Infection of Nlrp3-/- BMDMs resulted in delayed cell death and ~60% reduction in the calculated AUC.
source: However, infection of Nlrp3-/- BMDMs resulted in delayed cell death and ~60% reduction in the calculated AUC (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by real-time microscopy data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: IL-1β, Caspase-1, and GSDMD cleavage and release, which were induced in a T6SS3-dependent manner, were abrogated only in Nlrp3-/- BMDMs.
source: Furthermore, hallmark processes of inflammasome-mediated cell death, such as IL-1β, Caspase-1, and GSDMD cleavage and release, which were induced in a T6SS3-dependent manner, were abrogated only in Nlrp3-/- BMDMs (Figure 3b–d).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA and immunoblot data shown in Figure 3b-d.

claim: TNFα secretion was not affected in either Nlrp1-/- or Nlrp3-/- KO mouse BMDMs.
source: TNFα secretion, which was used as a control, was not affected in either of the KO mouse BMDMs (Figure 3b), thus confirming that priming (i.e. the NF-κB-dependent pathway) remained unaffected in the Nlrp3-/- BMDMs.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Complementation of tssL3 in trans restored the secretion of Hcp3.
source: The complementation of tssL3 in trans restored the secretion of Hcp3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), as well as all of the tested inflammasome-mediated phenotypes, including cell death and IL-1β, Caspase-1, and GSDMD cleavage and release (Figure 3e and f & Figure 3—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Complementation of tssL3 restored all tested inflammasome-mediated phenotypes including cell death and IL-1β, Caspase-1, and GSDMD cleavage and release.
source: The complementation of tssL3 in trans restored the secretion of Hcp3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), as well as all of the tested inflammasome-mediated phenotypes, including cell death and IL-1β, Caspase-1, and GSDMD cleavage and release (Figure 3e and f & Figure 3—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3e, f and Figure 3—figure supplement 1c,d.

claim: Over-expression of TssL3 had no effect on bacterial growth in MLB media.
source: Notably, over-expression of TssL3 had no effect on bacterial growth in MLB media (Figure 3—figure supplement 1f), but had a minor positive effect on bacterial growth in DMEM media (Figure 3—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1f.

claim: Over-expression of TssL3 had a minor positive effect on bacterial growth in DMEM media.
source: Notably, over-expression of TssL3 had no effect on bacterial growth in MLB media (Figure 3—figure supplement 1f), but had a minor positive effect on bacterial growth in DMEM media (Figure 3—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1f.

claim: T6SS3 activates a pyroptotic cell death program that is mediated directly by the NLRP3 inflammasome.
source: Thus, we concluded that T6SS3 activates a pyroptotic cell death program that is mediated directly by the NLRP3 inflammasome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic experiments with Nlrp3-/- and Mlkl-/- BMDMs.

claim: V. proteolyticus strains containing an active T6SS3 induced significant cell death in Gsdmd-/- BMDMs, albeit delayed compared to WT mice.
source: Using real-time microscopy, we found that in contrast with the negligible cell death observed upon infection of Nlrp3-/- BMDMs (Figure 4a and b), V. proteolyticus strains containing an active T6SS3 (i.e., Δvprh/Δhns1 and Δvprh/Δhns1/T6SS1-) induced a significant cell death in the absence of GSDMD, albeit delayed, compared to that observed in BMDMs from WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by real-time microscopy data shown in Figure 4a and b.

claim: IL-1β secretion from Gsdmd-/- BMDMs infected with Δvprh/Δhns1 or Δvprh/Δhns1/T6SS1- strain was comparable to that detected in BMDMs from WT mice.
source: Remarkably, IL-1β secretion from Gsdmd-/- BMDMs infected with the Δvprh/Δhns1 or the Δvprh/Δhns1/T6SS1- strain was comparable to that detected in BMDMs generated from WT mice (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: In Gsdmd-/- BMDMs, cleavage of Caspase-1, Caspase-3 (but not Caspase-8) and GSDME was observed, in addition to cleavage and release of IL-1β.
source: Moreover, while we detected the hallmark pyroptotic phenotypes in infected BMDMs generated from WT mice (i.e. cleaved and released Caspase-1, IL-1β, and GSDMD), in Gsdmd-/- BMDMs we observed the cleavage of Caspase-1, Caspase-3 (but not Caspase-8) and GSDME, in addition to cleavage and release of IL-1β (Figure 4d and e).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4d and e.

claim: In the absence of GSDMD, T6SS3 can induce a cell death cascade comprising Caspase-1, Caspase-3, and GSDME.
source: These results suggest that in the absence of GSDMD, T6SS3 can induce a cell death cascade comprising Caspase-1, Caspase-3, and GSDME.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed cleavage patterns in Gsdmd-/- BMDMs.

claim: GSDME can compensate, at least partially, for the absence of GSDMD.
source: Therefore, GSDME can compensate, at least partially, for the absence of GSDMD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell death and IL-1β secretion observed in Gsdmd-/- BMDMs.

claim: Activation of the alternative GSDME cascade still requires the NLRP3 inflammasome.
source: Notably, activation of this alternative cascade still requires the NLRP3 inflammasome, since cleaved Caspase-1, Caspase-3 and GSDME were absent in Nlrp3-/--derived BMDMs infected with the Δvprh/Δhns1 or Δvprh/Δhns1/T6SS1- strains (Figure 4d and e).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4d and e.

claim: VPR01S_RS02370 encodes a predicted transcription regulator belonging to the GlxA superfamily.
source: VPR01S_RS02370 is found at the edge of the T6SS3 gene cluster (Figure 5a), and it is transcribed in the opposite direction from its neighboring T6SS3 cluster gene, VPR01S_RS02375. VPR01S_RS02370 encodes a predicted transcription regulator belonging to the GlxA superfamily (according to the NCBI Conserved Domain Database Lu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis using the NCBI Conserved Domain Database.

claim: T6SS3 was dramatically induced upon Ats3 over-expression, as evident by elevated expression and secretion of Hcp3.
source: Importantly, we found that T6SS3 was dramatically induced upon Ats3 over-expression, as evident by elevated expression and secretion of Hcp3, whereas T6SS1 activity (determined by monitoring VgrG1 expression and secretion) remained unaltered (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: T6SS1 activity remained unaltered upon Ats3 over-expression.
source: Importantly, we found that T6SS3 was dramatically induced upon Ats3 over-expression, as evident by elevated expression and secretion of Hcp3, whereas T6SS1 activity (determined by monitoring VgrG1 expression and secretion) remained unaltered (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Over-expression of Ats3 had a stronger effect on T6SS3 activity than deletion of hns1.
source: Remarkably, over-expression of Ats3 had a stronger effect on T6SS3 activity than deletion of hns1 (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5b comparing secretion levels.

claim: Ats3 activates T6SS3 and not T6SS1.
source: These results suggest that Ats3 activates T6SS3 and not T6SS1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the selective induction of Hcp3 secretion.

claim: Over-expression of Ats3 had no effect on the antibacterial activity.
source: Interbacterial competition assays against sensitive E. coli prey (Ray et al., 2017) revealed that in contrast to the enhanced antibacterial activity seen upon deletion of hns1, which induces both T6SS1 and T6SS3, over-expression of Ats3 had no effect on the antibacterial activity (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial competition assay data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Over-expression of Ats3 did not confer antibacterial activity to a strain in which T6SS1 was inactivated.
source: Furthermore, over-expression of Ats3 did not confer antibacterial activity to a strain in which T6SS1 was inactivated (Δvprh/T6SS1-).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial competition assay data.

claim: T6SS3 does not play a role in interbacterial competition.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that Ats3 is a positive regulator of T6SS3, and that T6SS3 does not play a role in interbacterial competition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of antibacterial activity upon Ats3 over-expression.

claim: Over-expression of Ats3 induced a rapid, T6SS3-dependent cell death in BMDMs.
source: Using real-time microscopy, we found that over-expression of Ats3 from a plasmid (pAts3) induced a rapid, T6SS3-dependent cell death in BMDMs, which was similar to that induced upon hns1 deletion (Figure 5d and e & Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by real-time microscopy data shown in Figure 5d, e and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Infection of Nlrp3-/- BMDMs with Δvprh bacteria carrying pAts3 resulted in reduced cell death compared to infection of BMDMs from WT mice.
source: Moreover, infection of Nlrp3-/- BMDMs with Δvprh bacteria carrying pAts3 resulted in reduced cell death compared to that observed upon infection of BMDMs generated from WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by real-time microscopy data.

claim: IL-1β, Caspase-1, and GSDMD cleavage and release were induced in a T6SS3-dependent manner upon Ats3 over-expression.
source: In agreement, IL-1β, Caspase-1, and GSDMD cleavage and release were also induced, in a T6SS3-dependent manner, upon Ats3 over-expression (Figure 5f and g & Figure 5—figure supplement 1b)
evidence: This is supported by ELISA and immunoblot data shown in Figure 5f, g and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Addition of cytochalasin D abolished the pyroptosis induced by T6SS3 of a Δvprh V. proteolyticus strain over-expressing Ats3.
source: Indeed, we found that the addition of cytochalasin D, which inhibits phagocytosis by inhibiting actin polymerization (Brown and Spudich, 1979; Flanagan and Lin, 1980), abolished the pyroptosis induced by the T6SS3 of a Δvprh V. proteolyticus strain over-expressing Ats3 (Figure 6a, Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by real-time microscopy data shown in Figure 6a and Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Cytochalasin D abolished the weaker inflammasome-independent, T6SS3-dependent cell death observed upon infection of Nlrp3-/- BMDMs.
source: Interestingly, cytochalasin D also abolished the weaker inflammasome-independent, T6SS3-dependent cell death observed upon infection of Nlrp3-/- BMDMs.
evidence: This is supported by real-time microscopy data.

claim: Cytochalasin D did not abolish the cell death induced by T3SS1 of V. parahaemolyticus.
source: Notably, cytochalasin D did not abolish the cell death induced by T3SS1 of another pathogen, V. parahaemolyticus, which is independent of bacterial internalization (Burdette et al., 2008; Park et al., 2004) and was therefore used as a control (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b)
evidence: This is supported by real-time microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b and citations.

claim: The T6SS3-mediated pyroptotic cell death requires phagocytosis.
source: Combined, these results suggest that the T6SS3-mediated pyroptotic cell death requires phagocytosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cytochalasin D experiments.

claim: There was a dramatic advantage for V. proteolyticus with an active T6SS3 over a derivative strain with an inactive T6SS3 after 3 hr of BMDM infection.
source: Indeed, when we measured the bacterial load after 3 hr of BMDM infection, we observed a dramatic advantage for V. proteolyticus with an active T6SS3 (Δvprh +pAts3; parental strain) over a derivative strain with an inactive T6SS3 (T6SS3-) (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial count data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Bacterial counts were comparable between strains with active and inactive T6SS3 in the absence of BMDMs.
source: Notably, bacterial counts were comparable between the two strains in the absence of BMDMs (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial count data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: T6SS3 provides a survival advantage to V. proteolyticus upon its internalization by an immune cell.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that T6SS3 provides a survival advantage to V. proteolyticus upon its internalization by an immune cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on the bacterial survival data in BMDMs.

claim: Tie2 shares partial similarity with domains found at C-termini of polymorphic toxins.
source: Interestingly, hidden Markov model analyses (using the Jackhmmer server Potter et al., 2018) revealed that Tie2 shares partial similarity (in the region between amino acids 326 and 469) with domains found at C-termini of polymorphic toxins, such as proteins containing N-terminal LXG and WXG100 domains that are associated with type VII secretion systems (Tran et al., 2021; Whitney et al., 2017), as well as DUF4157 domains, which were recently suggested to carry toxins in extracellular contractile injection systems (Geller et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis using Jackhmmer and supported by citations.

claim: Tie1 and Tie2 were secreted in a T6SS3-dependent manner.
source: As shown in Figure 7a, Tie1 and Tie2 were secreted in a T6SS3-dependent manner, as was Hcp3; in contrast, secretion of VgrG1, a T6SS1 component, was unaffected by Ats3 over-expression.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Both Tie1 and Tie2 are T6SS3 secreted proteins.
source: These results confirm that both Tie1 and Tie2 are T6SS3 secreted proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the T6SS3-dependent secretion data.

claim: Deletion of both tie1 and tie2 in a Δvprh/Δhns1 background completely abolished the cell death and IL-1β secretion observed upon infection of BMDMs with the Δvprh/Δhns1 strain.
source: Remarkably, deletion of both tie1 and tie2 in a Δvprh/Δhns1 background (Δvprh/Δhns1/Δtie1/Δtie2) completely abolished the cell death and IL-1β secretion observed upon infection of BMDMs with the Δvprh/Δhns1 strain (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a,b), without affecting TNFα secretion (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by real-time microscopy and ELISA data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Deletion of tie1 alone resulted in an intermediate cell death phenotype.
source: Deletion of tie1 alone resulted in an intermediate cell death phenotype, whereas deletion of tie2 alone had no significant effect.
evidence: This is supported by real-time microscopy data.

claim: Deletion of tie2 alone had no significant effect on cell death.
source: Deletion of tie1 alone resulted in an intermediate cell death phenotype, whereas deletion of tie2 alone had no significant effect.
evidence: This is supported by real-time microscopy data.

claim: Over-expression of Tie1, either alone or together with Tie2, completely restored the cell death phenotype.
source: Complementation of Tie1 and Tie2 expression from a plasmid in the Δvprh/Δhns1/Δtie1/Δtie2 strain revealed that over-expression of Tie1, either alone (pTie1) or together with Tie2 (pTie1-2), completely restored the cell death phenotype, whereas bacteria over-expressing only Tie2 (pTie2) regained an intermediate ability to induce cell death (Figure 7b and c).
evidence: This is supported by real-time microscopy data shown in Figure 7b and c.

claim: Bacteria over-expressing only Tie2 regained an intermediate ability to induce cell death.
source: Complementation of Tie1 and Tie2 expression from a plasmid in the Δvprh/Δhns1/Δtie1/Δtie2 strain revealed that over-expression of Tie1, either alone (pTie1) or together with Tie2 (pTie1-2), completely restored the cell death phenotype, whereas bacteria over-expressing only Tie2 (pTie2) regained an intermediate ability to induce cell death (Figure 7b and c).
evidence: This is supported by real-time microscopy data shown in Figure 7b and c.

claim: Deletion of tie1, tie2, or both did not affect T6SS3 functionality, as evident by the secretion of Hcp3.
source: Importantly, deletion of tie1, tie2, or both did not affect T6SS3 functionality, as evident by the secretion of Hcp3 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1e)
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Deletion of tie1, tie2, or both did not affect bacterial growth or swimming motility.
source: it also did not affect bacterial growth or swimming motility (Figure 7—figure supplement 1f-g).
evidence: This is supported by growth and motility data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1f-g.

claim: Tie1 and Tie2 are T6SS3 effectors that are necessary to induce inflammasome-mediated cell death in BMDMs.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that Tie1 and Tie2 are T6SS3 effectors that are necessary to induce inflammasome-mediated cell death in BMDMs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the deletion and complementation experiments.

claim: Either Tie1 or Tie2 is sufficient to induce cell death, although the effect of Tie1 is more pronounced than that of Tie2.
source: Either protein is also sufficient to induce cell death, although the effect of Tie1 is more pronounced than that of Tie2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the complementation experiments.

claim: Highly similar T6SS clusters are found in other marine bacteria, including human pathogens such as V. parahaemolyticus and V. vulnificus.
source: Indeed, we identified highly similar T6SS clusters in other marine bacteria, including human pathogens such as V. parahaemolyticus and V. vulnificus (Baker-Austin et al., 2018), and marine animal pathogens such as Vibrio crassostreae (Bruto et al., 2017) and Vibrio anguillarum (Frans et al., 2011; Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis and shown in Figure 8, with citations.

claim: T6SS3-like clusters are often adjacent to DNA mobility elements such as integrases or transposases.
source: Interestingly, these T6SS3-like clusters are often adjacent to DNA mobility elements such as integrases or transposases, suggesting a mechanism for their spread via HGT.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of genomic neighborhoods.

claim: The identified T6SS3-like clusters carry a homolog of at least one of the inflammasome-inducing effectors, Tie1 or Tie2, at the edge of the cluster.
source: Notably, the identified T6SS3-like clusters carry a homolog of at least one of the inflammasome-inducing effectors, Tie1 or Tie2, at the edge of the cluster.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of the T6SS3-like clusters.

claim: T6SS3-like systems probably maintain their inflammasome-inducing activity.
source: Thus, these systems probably maintain their inflammasome-inducing activity, which may contribute to their pathogenic potential.
evidence: This is speculation based on the presence of Tie1/Tie2 homologs in these systems.

claim: EvpP from Edwardsiella tarda inhibits the NLRP3 inflammasome by targeting the MAPK-Jnk pathway.
source: Two other T6SS effectors were previously reported to indirectly affect inflammasome activation: EvpP from Edwardsiella tarda was shown to inhibit the NLRP3 inflammasome by targeting the MAPK-Jnk pathway (Chen et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: TecA from Burkholderia cenocepacia deamidates Rho GTPases, leading to activation of the pyrin-inflammasome.
source: whereas TecA from Burkholderia cenocepacia deamidates Rho GTPases, leading to activation of the pyrin-inflammasome (Aubert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: IL-1β release is one of the most ancient and conserved immune mechanisms.
source: Since IL-1β release is one of the most ancient and conserved immune mechanism (Dinarello, 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A recent study reported a similar compensation mechanism in the absence of GSDMD via chemical or Salmonella-induced NLRP3 inflammasome activation that also included Caspase-8 activation.
source: Notably, a recent study independently reported a similar compensation mechanism in the absence of GSDMD via chemical or Salmonella-induced NLRP3 inflammasome activation that also included Caspase-8 activation (Zhou and Abbott, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The cascade revealed in this work involves direct Caspase-3 activation by Caspase-1.
source: Therefore, we propose that the cascade revealed in our work involves direct Caspase-3 activation by Caspase-1, as was previously suggested for AIM2 inflammasome in the absence of Caspase-8 (Sagulenko et al., 2018).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed data and supported by citation.

claim: Vibrio coralliilyticus activates Caspase-3, leading to cleavage of GSDME and cell death in corals.
source: Indeed, Vibrio coralliilyticus was recently described to activate Caspase-3, leading to cleavage of GSDME and cell death in corals (Jiang et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A Caspase-1 homolog was previously described in Artemia sinica.
source: while a Caspase-1 homolog was previously described in Artemia sinica (Chu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The target of Tie1 and Tie2 is upstream of NLRP3.
source: Since NLR proteins, such as NLRP3, are less conserved in marine animals, we hypothesize that the target of Tie1 and Tie2 is upstream of NLRP3, and therefore the conservation between mammalian cells and marine animals lies in their ability to sense the effect of Tie1 and Tie2 activity as a danger signal that activates cell death pathways.
evidence: This is speculation based on the conservation of cell death mechanisms across species.

claim: The probable horizontal transfer of this anti-eukaryotic T6SS between marine bacteria may contribute to the emergence of new pathogenic Vibrio strains.
source: Finally, the probable horizontal transfer of this anti-eukaryotic T6SS between marine bacteria may also contribute to the emergence of new pathogenic Vibrio strains.
evidence: This is speculation based on the presence of DNA mobility elements near T6SS3-like clusters.
